documents.title: Start With a Plan
documents.summary: Start with one meaningful daily living skill. Identify what the learner already does well, what may be getting in the way, and what support could help. Build on strengths and interests rather than starting from deficits.
documents.aiSummary: Use when deciding where to begin. Help the caregiver choose one meaningful skill, identify the learner's existing strengths and interests, observe the specific barrier, and select support that directly matches that barrier.
aiTags: not sure which strategy to use
whenToUse: The caregiver is not sure where to begin.
A meaningful daily living skill needs to be selected.
The learner is struggling, but the specific barrier is not yet clear.

steps.title: Choose a meaningful life skill
steps.description: Choose something the learner values, wants to explore, or needs in everyday life.

steps.title: Notice strengths and barriers
steps.description: Identify what the learner can already do, what interests them, what helps them learn, which step is difficult, what gets in the way, and where support is needed.

steps.title: Build on what already works
steps.description: Use an existing strength or interest to support the next step of the new skill.

steps.title: Match support to the barrier
steps.description: Choose support that directly addresses the barrier.

useWhen: The user asks where to start.
The barrier has not yet been identified.
possibleSignals: I don't know where to start
notPrimaryWhen: The barrier and appropriate strategy are already clear.

documents.title: Task Analysis
documents.tagline: Make a big task easier, one step at a time.
documents.summary: Break a meaningful daily living skill into smaller, ordered steps and choose a teaching approach that matches the learner.
documents.aiSummary: Use Task Analysis when a daily living skill feels too large or has multiple steps. Break the task into small actions, put them in order, and teach them using forward chaining, backward chaining, or total-task practice.
whenToUse: A task has several steps.
The learner gets stuck partway through a routine.
The learner needs help remembering what comes next.

steps.title: Choose a skill
steps.description: Start with a skill the learner wants to learn.

steps.title: Break it into small steps
steps.description: Divide the task into manageable actions.

steps.title: Put the steps in order
steps.description: Create a clear sequence that becomes a roadmap for the skill.

steps.title: Choose how to teach
steps.description: Select forward chaining, backward chaining, or total-task practice.

useWhen: The learner loses their place or gets stuck in a sequence.
notPrimaryWhen: The learner already knows the sequence but lacks motivation.

documents.title: Consistent Practice
documents.summary: Use short, regular, predictable practice in everyday routines so skills become more familiar and independent over time.
documents.aiSummary: Use when a learner understands or has begun learning a skill but needs repetition to become more independent.
whenToUse: The learner has started learning a skill but performance is inconsistent.
The learner needs repetition to build fluency or confidence.

steps.title: Choose one meaningful skill
steps.description: Focus practice on one useful, meaningful skill.

steps.title: Practice briefly and regularly
steps.description: Use short practice opportunities instead of long or infrequent sessions.

steps.title: Keep support predictable
steps.description: Use familiar routines, similar prompts, and clear expectations.

steps.title: Celebrate growing independence
steps.description: Notice small wins and progress while giving the learner room to try.

useWhen: The learner can do at least part of the skill but needs repetition.
notPrimaryWhen: The learner does not yet understand the task.

documents.title: Prompting and Fading Prompts
documents.tagline: Offer support. Fade prompts. Build independence.
documents.summary: Provide a useful cue for the step that needs help, then intentionally reduce that support as the learner becomes more skilled.
documents.aiSummary: Use when the learner can participate in a skill but needs cues to complete a particular step. Select the least intrusive useful prompt, give time to respond, and reduce the prompt as skill increases.
whenToUse: The learner can perform a skill with reminders or cues.
One or more steps require extra support.

steps.title: Choose one meaningful skill
steps.description: Select the skill being practiced.

steps.title: Notice what the learner can already do
steps.description: Identify which parts are independent and which step needs support.

steps.title: Choose a helpful prompt
steps.description: Select a prompt that supports the difficult step without unnecessary help.

steps.title: Plan how support will be reduced
steps.description: Decide how the prompt can become shorter, lighter, or less frequent.

steps.title: Teach the step that needs help
steps.description: Use the selected prompt while allowing time to respond.

steps.title: Gradually fade the prompt
steps.description: Reduce the prompt as skill and confidence increase.

useWhen: The learner knows part of the skill but needs reminders.
possibleSignals: I have to remind them every time
notPrimaryWhen: The learner does not know how to perform the task at all.

documents.title: Step-by-Step Visual
documents.tagline: See the step. Do the step. Check what comes next.
documents.summary: Create a simple visual sequence with one action per image so the learner can follow a task with fewer verbal reminders.
documents.aiSummary: Use when the learner has difficulty remembering a sequence, relies heavily on verbal reminders, or benefits from visual information.
whenToUse: The learner benefits from visual information.
The learner forgets what comes next.
Verbal reminders are frequent.

steps.title: Choose an everyday skill
steps.description: Select the routine or task for the visual guide.

steps.title: Break the task into steps
steps.description: Identify the individual actions required.

steps.title: Create one visual for each step
steps.description: Use a clear image and short label for one action at a time.

steps.title: Put the visuals in order
steps.description: Arrange the images in task order.

steps.title: Model the task with the visual
steps.description: Demonstrate while pointing to the corresponding visual.

steps.title: Practice using the visual
steps.description: Encourage use of the visual rather than repeated verbal reminders.

useWhen: The learner responds better to pictures than repeated spoken instructions.
notPrimaryWhen: The primary issue is low motivation.

documents.title: Modeling
documents.tagline: Show the skill. Describe each step. Let your child try.
documents.summary: Demonstrate a clear action, pair it with simple language, and then give the learner an opportunity to practice what they observed.
documents.aiSummary: Use when verbal instructions alone are not enough or the learner needs to see what successful performance looks like.
whenToUse: The learner needs to see how an action is performed.
Spoken instructions are confusing or too abstract.

steps.title: Demonstrate one clear step
steps.description: Show the action in a simple and easy-to-observe way.

steps.title: Describe what you are doing
steps.description: Pair the demonstration with brief, concrete words.

steps.title: Let the learner watch, then practice
steps.description: Give the learner an opportunity to imitate or try the action.

steps.title: Show the step again when needed
steps.description: Repeat the model if another example is needed.

useWhen: The learner does not understand verbal directions alone.
The learner learns well by watching.
notPrimaryWhen: The learner already knows how to perform the skill and only needs motivation.

documents.title: Using Reinforcers
documents.summary: Connect practice with something meaningful to encourage participation, reinforce promptly, and gradually reduce tangible rewards as independence grows.
documents.aiSummary: Use when motivation or willingness to practice is a barrier. Identify something meaningful, connect practice to reinforcement, provide it promptly, and gradually reduce tangible rewards.
whenToUse: Motivation is a major barrier.
The learner understands the skill but is reluctant to practice.

steps.title: Choose something meaningful
steps.description: Identify praise, an activity, item, token, or other reinforcer that matters to the learner.

steps.title: Explain expectations clearly
steps.description: Make the practice expectation and what follows it easy to understand.

steps.title: Reinforce promptly
steps.description: Provide reinforcement soon after the target practice or skill occurs.

steps.title: Reduce tangible rewards gradually
steps.description: As independence develops, gradually rely less on tangible rewards.

useWhen: The learner knows what to do but has low motivation to practice.
notPrimaryWhen: The learner cannot do the task because of an access barrier.

documents.title: Incorporating Interests
documents.summary: Use preferred activities, hobbies, topics, characters, technology, or other interests to make daily living practice more meaningful and engaging.
documents.aiSummary: Use when a learner has difficulty engaging with practice but has identifiable interests. Connect the skill to preferred activities, themes, topics, or contexts.
whenToUse: The learner has identifiable interests that can be incorporated into practice.
Engagement or persistence is low.

steps.title: Identify meaningful interests
steps.description: Notice preferred activities, hobbies, topics, characters, technology, or other interests.

steps.title: Adapt materials
steps.description: Use a preferred theme or interest in practice materials.

steps.title: Choose an engaging context
steps.description: Practice the daily living skill through a favorite activity or meaningful setting.

steps.title: Use interests to reinforce success
steps.description: Connect successful practice with something the learner values when appropriate.

useWhen: The learner has strong interests that could support engagement.
notPrimaryWhen: A sensory or access barrier is the main reason participation is difficult.

documents.title: Using Relaxation Skills
documents.tagline: Calm the body. Make space for learning.
documents.summary: Teach and practice simple relaxation skills during calm moments so the learner has familiar tools for managing tension and emotional reactions.
documents.aiSummary: Use when physical tension, emotional reactions, or difficulty settling interfere with learning. Choose a relaxation strategy the learner will use and practice it during calm moments.
whenToUse: Stress, tension, or emotional reactions interfere with learning.
The learner becomes overwhelmed during practice.

steps.title: Personalize
steps.description: Choose a relaxation strategy the learner is willing to use.

steps.title: Show clearly
steps.description: Demonstrate the strategy using simple words and visuals when helpful.

steps.title: Practice often
steps.description: Practice during calm everyday moments so the strategy becomes familiar.

useWhen: Emotional or physical tension is interfering with learning.
notPrimaryWhen: Distress is caused by an unaddressed access barrier requiring accommodation.

documents.title: Tracking Progress & Problem Solving
documents.summary: Record what is working and what is difficult, identify the specific barrier when progress slows, and adjust the task or support to address that barrier.
documents.aiSummary: Use when progress has slowed, a strategy is not working, or caregivers are unsure why a particular step remains difficult.
whenToUse: Progress has slowed.
A strategy does not appear to be working.
One step remains difficult.

steps.title: Record what works and what is difficult
steps.description: Track independent steps, support needed, what went well, what was difficult, and adjustments tried.

steps.title: Identify the barrier
steps.description: Ask what is getting in the way and identify the exact difficult step.

steps.title: Adjust the task or support
steps.description: Choose an adjustment that directly matches the barrier and continue tracking.

useWhen: A selected strategy is not producing progress.
The caregiver can identify a difficult step but does not know why it is hard.
notPrimaryWhen: The learner is just beginning a skill and there is not enough practice information.

documents.title: Communication Scripts
documents.tagline: Start with a script. Grow their voice.
documents.summary: Use short, personalized words, phrases, questions, or sentence starters to give the learner a starting point for expressing needs, thoughts, feelings, or experiences.
documents.aiSummary: Use when the learner knows what they need or want but has difficulty finding the words, asking for help, or navigating everyday social communication.
whenToUse: The learner has difficulty finding words in everyday situations.
Asking for help or self-advocacy is difficult.

steps.title: Make it fit the learner
steps.description: Use the learner's words, communication style, and preferences.

steps.title: Keep it short and concrete
steps.description: Use simple, direct language that is easy to remember and use.

steps.title: Practice before the task
steps.description: Introduce the script, model it, try it together, and rehearse in a calm setting.

steps.title: Offer prompts when needed
steps.description: Use cue cards, checklists, or communication boards.

steps.title: Acknowledge and respond
steps.description: Respond positively, focusing on the message rather than perfect wording.

steps.title: Add details over time
steps.description: As confidence grows, encourage more detail and the learner's own words.

useWhen: The learner knows what they want to communicate but has trouble finding the words.
notPrimaryWhen: The main difficulty is completing physical or sequential task steps.

documents.title: Accommodations
documents.summary: Identify sensory, motor, cognitive, or language differences that affect participation and provide an alternative way to access the same broader learning goal.
documents.aiSummary: Use when a sensory, motor, cognitive, or language difference is preventing meaningful participation. Identify the actual barrier, find an alternative way to participate, prioritize engagement over compliance, and review supports over time.
whenToUse: A sensory, motor, cognitive, or language difference is interfering with participation.
Pressure to perform a task in one specific way is causing distress.

steps.title: Understand the barrier
steps.description: Determine what is getting in the way and distinguish a skill gap from an individual difference requiring accommodation.

steps.title: Prioritize meaningful participation
steps.description: Focus on learning and engagement rather than compliance with one specific method.

steps.title: Review and adjust supports
steps.description: Use accommodations to increase access and independence, then review them as needs and skills change.

useWhen: A sensory, motor, cognitive, or language difference prevents meaningful participation.
notPrimaryWhen: The learner can comfortably access the task but needs repetition, sequencing support, or motivation.
